newsitem.title: INDIA: India stages "successful" mock plane hijack.
newsitem.headline: India stages "successful" mock plane hijack.

text.p: Indian security agencies staged a bizarre mock plane hijacking on Thursday that the country's civil aviation chief described as a drill that successfully tested emergency systems.

"It was a pre-planned exercise involving the relevant security agencies," H.S. Khola, director-general of civil aviation, told a news conference after a five-hour exercise that left some senior officials confused.
Half an hour after news of the hijack of Alliance Air Flight 421A broke, a government spokesman told Reuters: "It is a mock exercise. It was meant to test the systems."
The strange saga began at 3.07 p.m. (0937 GMT) when the Alliance Air Boeing 737 took off from Delhi airport with 29 passengers and six crew.
"We took him (the pilot) into confidence immediately after take-off," Khola said. "Only the agencies who were required to be taken into confidence were told about it."
Alliance Air is a subsidiary of state-owned Indian Airlines.
Civil aviation authorities said the passengers aboard the unscheduled flight were government officials, including a woman, some of whom were not aware of the exercise.
Early reports about the mock hijacking confused even senior aviation officials who said the plane had been hijacked over the northern state of Punjab near India's border with Pakistan.
The authorities quickly denied the reports.

"There was a rumour that one Jammu-bound plane has been hijacked, but actually it was a mock exercise to get the response of the agencies involving anti-hijacking operations," a Civil Aviation Ministry spokeswoman told Reuters.
"The response was found to be good."

Keen to make the drill look realistic, authorities posted a sign at the Alliance Air counter saying: "Alliance Air flight 421A has been hijacked. For further information, kindly contact our control room."

"The exercise was all-encompassing," S.C. Tripathi, chief of civil aviation security told Reuters. "It involved the reflexes of security agencies, medical units, the police and the airline itself. We will have a full debriefing later."
Less than an hour after takeoff, the plane turned around over Punjab and headed back to the Indian capital.

"The message for hijacking was given at 4.05 p.m. (1035 GMT)," a Civil Aviation Ministry spokeswoman said. "The objective was to make it feel real, to check the effectiveness of the security systems."
At 4:30 p.m. (1100 GMT), the three "hijackers" demanded to speak to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, the spokeswoman said. Thirty-five minutes later, the aircraft landed safely in Delhi.

Indian Airlines official Anoop Arora said that once on the ground, the "hijackers" freed two passengers who had "fainted" and demanded that all vehicles be removed from around the aircraft, which was parked in a remote corner of the airport.

Alliance Air chief V. Kashyap told Reuters that the "hijackers" had been instructed to carry a gun and explosives, which they were to be allowed to take on board. "The whole thing was planned," he said.
An hour and a half after the plane landed, security chiefs of Alliance Air and airport authorities were holding simulated negotiations with the "hijackers" in the airline terminal.
Kashyap said the pilot and the "hijackers" were the only people on board aware that the operation was a drill. "The last such test was 11 years ago. It was essential to see how we would react."
